content:
Yesterday saw two conflicting reports about next year's iPhone, which is said to mark the 20th anniversary of the iPhone launch and is claimed to embody Apple's long-standing vision of "a single slab of glass."

We've had quite a few contradictory reports about what we'll actually see, but yesterday's divergence was the starkest yet...

Current situation

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive has often spoken about his long-term vision for the iPhone, hoping that the iPhone would eventually become a single piece of glass. It's widely believed that even with Ive's departure, Apple remains committed to this vision.

Although Apple generally doesn't make a big fuss about product anniversaries, the prevailing view is that they're aiming to realise this vision as closely as possible for the iPhone's 20th anniversary. This would very likely include embedding Face ID under the display, and possibly even hiding the front-facing camera beneath the screen.

However, we've seen quite a few conflicting reports. While the initial assumption was that this would be a standalone model, similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, more recent reports suggest this design would instead appear on next year's iPhone Pro models.

In sequence it would be the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple may skip that name for the anniversary and jump straight to iPhone 20.

Yesterday's contradictory reports

Yesterday things got even more confusing, as an analyst claimed that Apple has abandoned plans for an all-glass iPhone next year.

However, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman promptly came out to refute this claim.

The more likely scenario

The key point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone isn't a single endpoint. Whatever Apple plans to release next year, it will be one step—or several steps—towards that sci-fi "single piece of glass" vision.

The question isn't whether this goal can be achieved next year, but how far Apple will move towards this vision. But whether it's one step or several, this certainly won't be the final step in the iPhone's design evolution.

In fact, Gurman says Apple has already made compromises on what it had originally hoped to achieve next year.

The Jefferies analyst likely heard the same information, but being closer to the source, interpreted it as Apple having completely abandoned the plan.

My personal expectation is that next year's design will be a major leap—comparable to the big leap of the iPhone X—but there will be more developments in the years that follow. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will have made enough progress for Apple to adopt some kind of special branding, whether that's marking it as the 20th anniversary iPhone (which I think is unlikely), using some other special name, or skipping a generation and calling it the iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
